# (Radio)synthesis and in vitro-evaluation of dimeric FAP-inhibitor based radiopharmaceuticals

Marcel Martin, Sanjana Ballal, Madhav Yadav, Chandrasekhar Bal, Yentl Van Rymenant, Joni De Loose, Emile Verhulst, Ingrid De Meester, Pieter Van Der Veken and Frank Roesch

Journal of Nuclear Medicine June 2023, 64 (supplement 1) P64;

  * Article
  * Info & Metrics

## Abstract

P64

Introduction: Fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) is highly expressed in the tumor microenvironment by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in over 90% of epithelial carcinomas. Therefore, it is an ideal biological target for theranostic applications. Studies with radiopharmaceuticals based on the highly potent FAP inhibitor (FAPi) UAMC‑1110 as a targeting vector have shown great potential in molecular imaging but the short tumor retention time of the monomers (one targeting vector) do not match the half-lives of therapeutic radionuclides (^{177}Lu, ^{225}Ac, ^{90}Y). This could be improved by a dimer (two targeting vectors), however pharmacokinetic and radiolabeling properties still need further optimization.

This study aims to optimize our previously reported dimer by synthesizing the novel dimeric FAP inhibitor structures DOTA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2} and DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2}. Particular focus was directed to ^{225}Ac-labeling to enable targeted alpha-particle therapy (TAT) as well as investigating complex stabilities, lipophilicity and in vitro affinities.

Methods: DOTA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2} and DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2} were both synthesized and radiolabeled with ^{68}Ga and ^{177}Lu at 95 °C in 1 M HEPES buffer (pH = 4.5 or 5.5). The logD_{7.4} values were determined via shake-flask method. DOTA was further labeled with ^{90}Y under the same conditions (1 M HEPES buffer (pH = 4.5)) and DOTAGA was additionally radiolabeled with ^{225}Ac in 0.1 M sodium ascorbate (pH = 7.0) at 95 °C.

Complex stabilities of the radiolabeled compounds in human serum (HS) and phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) were investigated at 37 °C over two half-lives. In vitro affinity and selectivity was evaluated by determining the IC_{50} values of each molecule for FAP, prolyl endopeptidase (PREP) and the dipeptidyl peptidases (DPP) DPP4, DPP8 and DPP9.

Results: Both compounds were labeled successfully with ^{68}Ga (RCC > 95% after 5 min) and also with ^{177}Lu (10-20 nmol/GBq) in quantitative RCC > 99%. DOTA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2} was further labeled with ^{90}Y with similar results compared to ^{177}Lu. All radiolabeled products were stable over 2 half-lives in HS and PBS and the hydrophilicity was high for DOTA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2} but even higher for DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2}.

For [^{225}Ac]Ac-DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2} the labeling yield reached 90-95% after 15 min with 30-40 nmol/MBq. The final formulation was stable. The stability was also high in HS over 20 days and in PBS for at least 2 days.

In vitro studies showed very high affinity for FAP (<1 nM) and high selectivity over the related proteases (PREP and DPPs) for both compounds.

The first study in a patient with medullary thyroid cancer was carried out. The patient was previously treated with [^{177}Lu]Lu-DOTAGA.(SA.FAPi)_{2}, where besides high uptake and long tumor retention a high uptake in the liver (at 24 h p.i.) and colon (48 h p.i.) was observed. In contrast, the new compound [^{177}Lu]Lu-DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2} showed negligible liver and colon uptake at 24 h p.i. besides high tumor uptake.

Conclusions: Especially the novel FAPi dimer DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2} showed improved radiolabeling properties compared to the DOTA derivative and first-generation FAPi dimer DOTAGA.(SA.FAPi)_{2}. For both new compounds the in vitro affinity and selectivity were superior to those of DOTAGA.(SA.FAPi)_{2} which made them promising candidates for improved theranostic application. A first proof-of-concept in vivo study suggested that [^{177}Lu]Lu-DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPi)_{2} is an ideal candidate for in vivo application with superior pharmacological properties compared to DOTAGA.(SA.FAPi)_{2} with a significantly reduced radiotracer uptake to the non-target and critical organs (liver, colon) while maintaining the long tumor retention time.

## RESULTS

### Patient Characteristics

The clinical characteristics of the study population are summarized in Table 1 and Supplemental Table 1 (supplemental materials are available at http://jnm.snmjournals.org). Between October 2020 and 2022, 200 patients were included, 91 (45%) women and 109 (55%) men. Of the 200 patients, 65 (33%) had BS and 135 (67%) had STS; 141 (70%) cases were high grade, 32 (16%) cases were low grade, and 27 (14%) cases had no World Health Organization grade (NA). Patients underwent clinical ^{68}Ga-FAPI PET imaging for either staging (49/200 [25%]) or follow-up (151/200 [75%]). Fourteen (7%) patients were imaged with ^{68}Ga-FAPI-04, and 186 (93%) were imaged with ^{68}Ga-FAPI-46. All patients imaged with ^{68}Ga-FAPI-46 underwent ^{18}F-FDG PET imaging within 4 wk. No PET-related adverse events were reported.

Preliminary studies in small cohorts of patients have shown increased FAP PET signal in a wide range of settings including cardiac injury, interstitial lung disease and pulmonary fibrosis, IgG4-related disease, cirrhosis, renal injury, inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis (18–21).
Metastatic brain tumors are shown to have increased uptake on FAP PET, although there is currently no evidence demonstrating a benefit of FAP PET compared to standard modalities for the evaluation of primary brain tumors. In head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, FAP PET appears to reduce false positive results obtained by FDG with respect to regional nodal metastases (11). One of the main regions with decreased physiologic uptake could be in peritoneal imaging, where bowel activity limits FDG PET, and this has been shown to be beneficial in ovarian cancer and gastric cancer (12,13).

On the other hand, several cancer types do not induce a strong and/or consistent FAP uptake such as lymphoma, myeloma, prostate adenocarcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, melanoma and seminoma. It is unlikely that FAP PET will play a significant role in staging of these cancers. Lastly, tumors of mesenchymal origin express FAP on both CAFs and tumor cells, which is of particular interest in sarcomas. Although sarcomas can have high uptake on FAP PET, it does not appear to improve staging compared to FDG PET, and its role may be limited to sarcomas with low FDG avidity and high FAP expression (e.g. solitary fibrous tumor) and selection for radioligand therapy (RLT) (14).

Evaluating the use of FAP PET for treatment response is in its early stages, but early studies suggest that FAP PET can accurately measure response to treatment (15,16). Although treatment-induced fibrosis, inflammation and necrosis could represent challenges for this indication, this may be limited to treatments that induce fibrotic responses such as external beam radiation therapy. Additionally, surgery can result in fibrosis seen on FAP PET that can persist for up to 8 months (17). With the future approval of FAP targeted therapies, both RLTs and non-RLT therapies, the role of FAP PET as a biomarker for therapeutic target assessment may become important.

# Comparative Evaluation of 18F-FDG and 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT for Imaging Metastatic Soft Tissue Sarcoma

Shamim ahmed Shamim, Yogita Khandelwal, Bela Jain, Swapnil Yadav, Sameer Rastogi and Naresh Kumar

Journal of Nuclear Medicine June 2025, 66 (supplement 1) 252150;

## Abstract

252150

Introduction: Fibroblast activation protein (FAP) is overexpressed on the surface of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF) and tumor cells across various malignancies, including sarcoma. While ^{18}F-FDG PET/CT has been established as a valuable imaging tool for staging, restaging, treatment monitoring, and prognostication in metastatic soft tissue sarcoma (STS), its sensitivity is suboptimal for certain sarcoma subtypes, particularly low-grade tumors. This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic utility of ^{68}Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT in patients with metastatic STS, comparing its performance to that of ^{18}F-FDG PET/CT.

Methods: This prospective study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital's Nuclear Medicine and Medical Oncology departments (study is ongoing). A total of 18 patients (8 females, 10 males; median age 32 years, range 16–68) with metastatic STS were enrolled. All patients underwent both ^{18}F-FDG and ^{68}Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT within one week using Siemens Biograph mCT 64 or GE Discovery 710 scanners. Imaging data were analyzed visually and semi-quantitatively, assessing the number of lesions, maximum standardized uptake values (SUVmax), and tumor-to-background ratios (TBR). The Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test was used to compare semi-quantitative metrics (SUVmax, TBR), while the McNemar test was applied to evaluate differences in lesion detection between the two tracers.

Results: Among the 18 patients, 7 distinct subtypes of STS were identified. Compared to ^{18}F-FDG PET/CT, ^{68}Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT detected a higher number of metastatic lesions (132 vs. 112). The mean ± standard deviation (SD) SUVmax values were 6.2 ± 3.6 for ^{18}F-FDG and 5.4 ± 2.6 for ^{68}Ga-FAPI-46, with no significant difference (p > 0.05). Discordant findings between the two tracers were observed, particularly in liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, and alveolar soft tissue sarcoma, where ^{68}Ga-FAPI-46 showed more favorable uptake.

Conclusions: ^{68}Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT emerges as a promising imaging modality for detecting metastatic lesions in STS, offering comparable diagnostic performance to ^{18}F-FDG PET/CT. Notably, certain STS subtypes may benefit from ^{68}Ga-FAPI-46’s enhanced sensitivity. Larger, multicenter studies are needed to further validate these findings and establish its role in clinical practice.

## NEW TARGETS

In addition to hydroxyapatite, somatostatin receptors, and the prostate-specific membrane antigen, there are additional targets under investigation for their utility in TAT. One of the most prominent new targets is the fibroblast activation protein (FAP) that is overexpressed by cancer-associated fibroblasts in the stroma of several tumor entities as well as less frequently directly from tumor cells. FAP can be targeted with antibodies, peptides, and small molecules such as FAP inhibitors (FAPIs). FAP-targeted imaging has been explored in several malignancies, including glioma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, soft-tissue sarcoma, pancreatic cancer, breast cancer, and prostate cancer (47). Research into the therapeutic application of FAPI radionuclides is still in the early stages. Breast cancer patients have been treated with ^{90}Y-FAPI-04 (48) and ^{177}Lu-DOTA.SA.FAPI (49), an ovarian cancer patient has been treated with ^{90}Y-FAPI-46 (50), and sarcoma and pancreatic cancer patients have been treated with ^{90}Y-FAPI-46 (50) and ^{177}Lu-FAPI-46.
